Who sets the value on an Ohio tax bill?

Each county auditor appraises the parcels in that county, and your bill starts from the auditor's figure. The state tax department describes a complete reappraisal on a six year cycle. In between, a lighter update every third year leans on sales data instead of a site visit.

A millage rate then turns value into dollars. Inside mills come from local governments without a ballot. Outside mills come from levies voters approved for schools, fire districts and similar services. So a bill can rise even when your house is valued the same, since a fresh levy lifts the rate. The Board of Revision hears disputes over value only. The rate is off the table.

The Department of Taxation property tax page outlines two ways to question the figure. A handful of counties offer an informal review, mostly in reappraisal years. All of them take the formal complaint. Phone the auditor to find out what your parcel qualifies for.

Due dates and penalties

You may settle an Ohio bill in a lump sum or in installments. Under R.C. 323.12, paying everything at once is due by the final day of December. Choosing halves means the first half (plus any older delinquency) is due then, with the balance following on June 20 of the next year. Real bills often show later dates, because R.C. 323.17 moves payment to January 31 and July 20 when the duplicate reaches the treasurer late. Your own bill is the final word on dates.

Money has to reach the treasurer by the deadline, or be mailed with a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated on or before it. Private meter stamps are rejected. Some treasurers hold the books open a short while to process the mail.

The penalty schedule in R.C. 323.121 works like this:

  • Late on the first half: ten percent is added to the unpaid half.
  • Late on the second half: another ten percent lands on whatever current tax is still unpaid.
  • After that, back taxes earn interest at the rate set under section 5703.47.

Appealing your assessment

You begin at the auditor's counter, and the auditor forwards the complaint to the Board of Revision. Under R.C. 5715.19 you have until the later of two dates: the end of March following the tax year at issue, or the day the treasurer wraps up first-half collections. A mailed complaint is judged by its postmark.

Besides the owner, the statute names the owner's spouse, a retained assessment professional, a retained accountant, appraiser or real estate broker, and in some commercial leases the tenant. Bring comparable sales, any independent appraisal you hold, and recent photographs of the house.

You cannot refile within the same interim period unless a new event occurred after the lien date. The qualifying events are:

  • An arm's length sale of the property.
  • A casualty loss of value.
  • A substantial improvement.
  • An occupancy change of fifteen percent or more that hits the property's economics hard.

Still unhappy? The Board of Tax Appeals hears the next round. R.C. 5717.01 sets a thirty day limit that runs from the date the county board mails its notice.

Homestead exemption

A homestead exemption trims the tax on a house you occupy. R.C. 323.152 covers owners who are permanently and totally disabled, owners sixty-five or older, certain surviving spouses, disabled former service members, and the surviving spouses of public service officers killed on duty. Under R.C. 323.151, the protected home includes up to one acre around the dwelling. Anyone who turned sixty-four before January 1 of the application year satisfies the age test.

The basic reduction protects twenty-five thousand dollars of true value, and the tax commissioner adjusts it for inflation. Disabled former service members and surviving spouses of officers killed on duty receive fifty thousand dollars and face no income test. Other applicants must stay under an income ceiling that the statute states as thirty thousand dollars of total income, also indexed each year. Ask the auditor for today's figure.

A second layer applies to any homestead. The statute sets percentages of the tax from qualifying levies. The first tax year the amendment applies earns 5.70 percent, then 8.92 percent, then 12.15 percent, and finally 15.38 percent from the third following year onward. Ask the auditor which step your year falls on.

Applications go to the auditor's office. Most owners use Form DTE 105A, DTE 105I is for disabled former service members and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K is for officers' surviving spouses. Once approved, you remain enrolled until eligibility changes. The owner-occupancy credit is a separate benefit for a primary residence you occupied on the January 1 of the application year.

Selling with taxes owed

Each year's tax lien fastens to the land on January 1 and remains until the tax, penalties and interest are cleared, as R.C. 323.11 puts it. A new deed leaves the lien intact. Either the unpaid amount is paid from your sale proceeds or the buyer takes it on. Get a payoff figure from the county treasurer before closing.

The deed step brings one more form. Under R.C. 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value with the auditor, which must say whether the homestead exemption cut your taxes and whether the land was valued for current agricultural use. A buyer who cannot claim a break you enjoyed will see a different next bill.

Owners already behind have an escape route. R.C. 323.31 guarantees an occupant owner a single written delinquent tax contract with the county treasurer. Installments can stretch up to five years, and to at least two if the owner requests it. A missed installment or unpaid current tax voids the deal, and none is available while a tax certificate or foreclosure judgment stands.

Planning a fast sale? Request the treasurer's payoff figure first, then have the title company confirm the lien gets paid from proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can often close quickly enough to clear a delinquency before any foreclosure judgment.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Ohio Board of Revision complaint deadline?

The later of two dates: the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection ends. File with the auditor, who forwards it. A mailed complaint is dated by its postmark.

Can I split my Ohio property tax bill?

Yes. You can split the bill into two halves, one near year end and one in June. A late duplicate shifts both into January and July, so rely on the dates printed on your bill.

Can I get a homestead exemption if I am under sixty-five?

Yes, when you are permanently and totally disabled on January 1 of the application year, or when you are a disabled former service member or qualifying surviving spouse. Any homestead also gets a partial exemption. The county auditor takes applications.

Who sets the Ohio millage rate?

Local governments set inside mills, and voters approve outside mills through levies. A valuation complaint cannot change the rate. Only the property's value can be challenged at the Board of Revision.

What if I cannot pay my Ohio property tax on a home I live in?

Ask the county treasurer for a delinquent tax contract. A resident owner is entitled to one, with payments spread over as many as five years. Signing before a foreclosure judgment stops the county from suing while you keep up the installments.

Who qualifies for the Ohio homestead exemption

The exemption goes to owner-occupants who are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, or the surviving spouse of someone in those groups. A disabled veteran, a disabled veteran's surviving spouse, and the surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty get their own larger reduction. The definitions sit in R.C. 323.151.

Age is counted in a particular way. For this purpose, "sixty-five years of age or older" means a person who reached 64 before January 1 of the year of application. In practice a senior owner must be 65 by December 31 of the year the application is filed.

The home itself has to meet several tests:

  • It is a dwelling the applicant owns and occupies as a home, with Ohio as the domicile.
  • It includes the surrounding land only up to one acre that is reasonably needed for the home.
  • It was not acquired from a relative, other than a spouse, for the purpose of qualifying.
  • An owner can be a life tenant, a vendee in possession under a land contract, a mortgagor, or the settlor of a trust that holds title to a home the settlor occupies.

Homes held by corporations, partnerships and LLCs generally do not qualify, because the owner is not an individual.

How much the exemption takes off the bill

It works as a credit on the property tax bill, figured on a slice of the home's market value. The size of the credit also depends on the local tax rate: the higher the rate, the higher the credit. The reduction amounts are indexed for inflation each year.

Homestead reduction amounts and income limit, tax year 2026 (real property)
Owner groupTax year 2026 amount
Low-income senior or disabled owner$29,700
Disabled veteran, or surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty$59,400
Income threshold for seniors and disabled owners$41,000

Income is measured by modified adjusted gross income, which the statute defines for the owner and spouse for the year before the application.

No income test applies to a disabled veteran, a disabled veteran's surviving spouse, or the surviving spouse of a public service officer. Owners who received the exemption in 2013, before means testing returned, are also outside the income test.

Where and when to file

File with the auditor of the county where the home sits, on or before December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Three forms are in use: DTE 105A for most applicants, DTE 105I for a disabled veteran or that veteran's surviving spouse, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers. Every county auditor must take a paper copy, and some accept electronic filing.

A disability claim needs a certificate. R.C. 323.153 calls for a physician's certificate for a physical disability, and a physician or psychologist who practices in Ohio for a mental one. A certificate from a state or federal agency that classifies disability also works. A veteran attaches written confirmation of the disability rating from the federal VA.

After filing, the sequence runs like this:

  • The auditor approves or denies the application and sends notice within thirty days of that decision.
  • A denial notice must state the reasons.
  • An owner who thinks the denial was wrong, or the reduction too small, can appeal to the county board of revision within sixty days of the notice, using form DTE 106B.
  • Each January the auditor mails a continuing application. Send it back only if ownership, occupancy, disability or income changed.

A false statement made to get the reduction is a fourth-degree misdemeanor and bars the reduction for three years after a conviction.

What happens to the exemption when you sell

The reduction follows the owner, not the house. Under R.C. 323.152(C), a transfer of ownership after an application was filed does not forfeit the reduction for that year. Once the home is sold, though, the seller no longer owns or occupies it, so the continuing application should go back to the auditor reporting the change.

Failing to report costs money. If the auditor or treasurer finds that an owner kept a reduction after losing eligibility, a charge goes on the property for each affected tax year, with interest as if the reduction were delinquent tax. It is collected like delinquent taxes, which makes it something a title company will catch at closing.

The buyer starts from a different place. The partial exemption in R.C. 323.152(B)(2) calls for a fresh application when a home changed hands in the preceding year, and the auditor mails an original application each February for homes that transferred. The filing deadline is again December 31. A senior or disabled buyer who moves in must apply at the new address, beginning in January of the year after the move. Ownership and occupancy as of January 1 decide the tax year.

Other Ohio property tax reductions

Three other pieces of relief show up on Ohio residential bills. The first is the partial exemption under R.C. 319.302, which the auditor reviews parcel by parcel as of January 1. For residential property it is listed at seven and one-half percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, with later steps ending at zero percent for and after the third following tax year. Ask the auditor what percentage applies to a given bill.

The second is the owner-occupancy credit, a reduction on a primary residence occupied on January 1 of the application year. Ask the auditor whether it already appears on your bill.

The third is a county option created by House Bill 96, signed in June 2025. County commissioners may adopt a local-option homestead exemption that mirrors the state one, with the same eligibility rules and the same amount. Nobody applies for it separately: anyone already getting the state exemption receives it automatically once a county turns it on. The auditor can tell you whether your county has done so.

Farmland has its own track, the Current Agricultural Use Value program, which also runs through the auditor.

Selling a house that has the exemption

The exemption rarely changes the sale itself, but it shows up in the tax figures on the settlement statement. A seller who has been receiving the credit should bring the most recent tax bill to closing, since the credit appears there. A buyer who plans to live in the house should ask the title company how the owner-occupancy filing is handled at the county auditor's conveyance step.

A few practical points for sellers:

  • An heir who inherits a home does not get the seller's reduction automatically. Eligibility depends on the new owner's own age, disability and occupancy.
  • A home under a land contract can still qualify, because R.C. 323.151 counts a vendee in possession as an owner.
  • Pending appeals and unpaid installments are matters for the county treasurer, who bills and collects the tax.

Back taxes, a tenant or heavy repairs are separate problems from the exemption. A cash sale skips showings and repair negotiations, and the title company still handles any tax proration at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to reapply for the Ohio homestead exemption every year?

No. Once approved, the application continues for each year the dwelling is your homestead. The auditor mails a continuing application each January, and you return it only if your income, ownership, occupancy or disability status changed.

What is the last day to file the Ohio homestead exemption for real property?

December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Manufactured and mobile homes taxed that way file by December 31 of the year before. The statute allows a late application for the preceding year to be filed with an original application.

Can I get the Ohio homestead exemption if my home is in a trust?

Often yes. Revocable and irrevocable trusts can qualify when the trust gives you complete possession of the property. Check the trust language with the county auditor before applying.

Who decides the Ohio homestead exemption, and where do I appeal?

The county auditor decides it. If you believe the denial or the amount is wrong, file a complaint with the county board of revision within sixty days of the auditor's notice.

Does selling my Ohio home end the exemption?

Yes, for future years. The reduction applies to a home you own and occupy, so tell the auditor when you no longer qualify. Skipping that step can lead to a charge on the property with interest for years the reduction should not have been given.

How an Ohio foreclosure ends in a sheriff sale

The lender sues in the county court of common pleas, wins a judgment, and the court orders the property sold. Under R.C. 2323.07 the court can order a tract sold whole or in parcels. When land spans several counties, it can direct the sheriff of each county, or a single officer, to make the sale. Chapter 2329 then governs how the sale runs.

Once you are served with the lawsuit, the home could be lost in three to six months. Open every piece of mail from the court, call your servicer right away, and stay in the house. Living there keeps the home in better shape, and the lender prefers it that way until the sheriff says otherwise.

Free help is a phone call away: Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, the Ohio Department of Commerce at 800-750-0750, Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446, and HUD approved counselors at 888-995-HOPE.

Appraisal before the sale

The sheriff summons three disinterested freeholders, who must live in the county and own real property there, to appraise the land by viewing it. For a residence, R.C. 2329.17 gives them twenty-one calendar days from the clerk's order to return a value. If they run past that window, they go unpaid, the appraised value becomes the auditor's latest value, and the sale proceeds. A court can approve a separate appraisal for good cause.

The municipality or township may also inspect any structures on the land before the sale. The sheriff's office can tell you whether an inspection has been set for your property.

The appraisal sets the floor for the first auction. Under R.C. 2329.20, land cannot sell for less than two-thirds of its appraised value, subject to exceptions in sections 2329.51 and 2329.52. A junior lienholder enforcing against land that carries a prior lien faces a modified minimum set by the court.

Notice requirements

Two kinds of notice are needed. Under R.C. 2329.26, the creditor or its lawyer must serve written notice on the judgment debtor and every other party, and file it with proof of service at least seven calendar days ahead of the sale. A party in default for failing to appear need not be served. The officer must also advertise once a week for at least three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county.

The ad gives the date, time and place, or for an online sale the start date, minimum length and web address. It also states the required deposit and warns bidders that they answer for any costs, allowances and taxes the proceeds fall short of covering.

These rules have teeth. Under R.C. 2329.27, a sale made without the required notices is set aside on motion of an interested party. After the court confirms a sale, though, the order counts as a finding that notice was adequate and bars further motions to set the sale aside. If you spot a notice defect, raise it before confirmation.

Deposits and the second auction

Any bidder other than the foreclosing lender must put down a deposit tied to the home's appraised value. R.C. 2329.211 sets three tiers for residential property:

  • Two thousand dollars when the appraisal is ten thousand dollars or less.
  • Five thousand dollars when the appraisal is above ten thousand and up to two hundred thousand.
  • Ten thousand dollars when the appraisal is above two hundred thousand.

A purchaser who misses the deposit timing voids the sale, and the home may move to a provisional second sale if one was announced.

When a house in a residential mortgage foreclosure fails to sell at the first auction, R.C. 2329.52 calls for a second auction between seven and thirty days later. The highest bidder wins with no minimum bid, although costs, allowances and real estate taxes must still be covered. If the house is unsold after two auctions, it may be offered again without the minimum or disposed of another way the chapter allows.

Steps from judgment to deed

StageWhat happens

AppraisalThree freeholders, twenty-one days for a home
First auctionMinimum bid of two-thirds of appraised value

ConfirmationWithin thirty days of the return of the writ
RedemptionAny time before confirmation

Redeeming or stopping an Ohio sheriff sale

You can redeem until the court confirms the sale. R.C. 2329.33 lets the debtor deposit with the clerk the judgment amount, all costs, and interest at eight percent a year on the purchase money from the day of sale. The court then sets the sale aside, applies the deposit to the judgment and awards the interest to the bidder. After confirmation, redemption under that section is over.

Timing is tight. Under R.C. 2329.31, the court reviews the sale and journalizes confirmation within thirty days of the return of the writ, though it may stay confirmation to let an owner redeem. The buyer then has thirty days after confirmation to pay the balance, and the officer records the deed within fourteen days after confirmation and payment. If the deed is late, the buyer can ask for a court order that works as the deed. The county auditor then updates ownership for tax purposes, and taxes that come due after the sale fall on the new owner.

Selling the house yourself can produce the redemption money. Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a written payoff, check the docket with the clerk, and keep the confirmation date in view. A cash buyer who can close before confirmation gives you a way to pay off the judgment and keep whatever equity remains.

Mediation is another route. A foreclosure case can be mediated anywhere from before filing up to confirmation of the sale, and it has even been done after the sheriff sale. Programs vary by county court, so call the court. After a sale, proceeds generally go in this order: the court, the sheriff, the county treasurer, then lienholders, with any remainder going to the owner. Beware firms that charge fees for services available for free. Save the Dream Ohio referrals cost nothing.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a sheriff sale take after a foreclosure judgment in Ohio?

The statutes set pieces, not one total. Appraisal takes up to twenty-one days, advertising runs at least three weeks, confirmation follows within thirty days of the writ's return, and the buyer has thirty days to pay. The clerk can give you the dates on your case.

What is the minimum bid at an Ohio sheriff sale?

Two-thirds of the appraised value at the first auction. In a residential mortgage foreclosure, a second auction held seven to thirty days later has no minimum bid. Costs and real estate taxes still have to be covered.

Can I redeem my Ohio home after the sheriff sale?

Only before the court confirms the sale. You deposit the judgment amount, costs and eight percent interest on the purchase money with the clerk. Once confirmed, that right ends.

Do I have to move out before the Ohio sheriff sale?

No. Owners are urged to stay in the home and keep it in good condition until the sheriff says they must leave.

Where can I get free help with an Ohio foreclosure?

Call Save the Dream Ohio at 888-404-4674, or the Ohio State Legal Services Association at 866-529-6446. HUD approved counselors are at 888-995-HOPE. Your county common pleas court can tell you whether it offers foreclosure mediation.

Does Ohio charge an estate tax?

No. House Bill 153 repealed the Ohio estate tax for every estate with a date of death in 2013 or later. House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly then closed the books on older estates: nothing is owed on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported by that date.

A family selling an inherited Ohio house therefore files no state estate tax return before closing. The state has also dropped the requirement for ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms before a decedent's assets move to another person, and county auditors and banks have been asked to stop forwarding them.

Federal estate tax

Only a very large estate owes it. The basic exclusion amount for a 2026 death is $15,000,000, a figure raised by Public Law 119-21, which was signed July 4, 2025. One house rarely comes close, so for most families the federal return does not set the timeline.

Two further points apply. An estate that does not have to file a federal return should skip Form 8971. When a spouse survives, the estate may elect on a timely return to hand the unused exclusion to that spouse.

Who signs the deed on an inherited Ohio house

Usually the executor or administrator, working under the probate court of the decedent's home county. Ohio's land-sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians runs from R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43. An executor whose will grants a power of sale may follow the will instead.

Smaller estates may skip full administration. R.C. 2113.03 lets the court release an estate from administration at $35,000 in assets or under. The ceiling is $100,000 if a surviving spouse takes everything. The order can direct delivery of personal property and transfer of real property, and the court may name a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers. A buyer who pays value in good faith gets the same protection from unsecured creditors that administration would give.

  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate fits a release or needs letters of authority.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, and the vesting deed.
  • Order a title search early so liens surface before a buyer finds them.

Transfer on death affidavits

Title may already belong to a named beneficiary. Under R.C. 5302.22, an owner may record a verified transfer on death designation affidavit with the county recorder while still alive. When the owner dies, title vests in the beneficiaries the affidavit names.

Nobody has to pay for it or receive it for it to work. The recorder charges the deed fee and files it under the owner's name. Heirs who think a parent signed one should ask the recorder to search that name. Knowingly false statements in the affidavit count as falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

Taxes when an heir sells the house

An heir's taxable gain starts from basis. For inherited property that is generally the fair market value on the date of death. Estates that elected the alternate valuation date use that figure instead, and farm or business land can use special-use valuation. An heir who never received a Schedule A (Form 8971) from the executor can rely on the appraised date-of-death value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

Order an appraisal early and keep it with the estate papers so the tax preparer can apply it to the final price.

Who handles each step of an inherited-house sale in Ohio
StepOffice and statute
Release from administration or land saleProbate court, R.C. 2113.03 and R.C. 2127.01
Transfer on death affidavit searchCounty recorder, R.C. 5302.22
County transfer tax paid at deed deliveryCounty auditor, R.C. 322.02
Valuation complaintCounty auditor, then board of revision, R.C. 5715.19

R.C. 322.02 caps any county transfer levy at thirty cents for each hundred dollars of value. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office before the deed is recorded. Ask the county auditor which rate your house falls under.

Challenging the county's value

An owner can. R.C. 5715.19 routes a valuation complaint through the county auditor. The filing date is March 31 of the following tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. The county board of revision decides it. A second complaint on the same parcel in the same interim period is barred unless conditions changed. Examples are an arm's length sale, a casualty loss or a substantial improvement.

A date-of-death appraisal can support a complaint when the county figure looks high. The auditor's office can tell you which tax year a new filing would cover.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ohio houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What buyers and title companies ask the estate for

The first thing a title company wants is proof of who can sign. It will not insure a deed whose chain it cannot follow. For an estate in administration, that is the executor's or administrator's letters of authority from the probate court. For a released estate, it is a copy of the release order. If a transfer on death affidavit covers the house, bring the recorded affidavit and a death certificate.

The title company will also search for mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax. Ohio land sales by fiduciaries follow the statute, so a sale that skips the court steps can leave a buyer with a cloud on title. If the file is tangled, a probate attorney in the home county can confirm which documents the closing will need before you accept an offer.

Where an Ohio heir should start

Begin with whatever decides who may sign, then turn to the house. The probate clerk is the first call.

  • Find the original will and file it with the probate court if no one has.
  • Keep the house insured and secured, and redirect the mail.
  • Ask the recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit exists.
  • Request the current tax bill from the county treasurer.
  • Order the date-of-death appraisal.

Timeline for planning: the probate clerk's answer on authority comes first, since nothing can be listed with confidence until you know who signs. A title search and the payoff of any mortgage follow. Valuation questions and the county transfer tax can be sorted out in parallel. A buyer who pays cash does not need a lender to approve the estate's paperwork, but the title company still does, so gather the letters or release order before you list.

When the family wants out fast, a cash buyer who accepts the house in its current condition can remove the repair list and the open houses. If that fits, compare offers by what the estate keeps after transfer tax, payoffs and costs. Those items apply whichever way the house sells, so the real difference is time and certainty.

Frequently asked questions

Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?

No. The tax was repealed for estates with a 2013 or later date of death, and the House Bill 110 sunset ended collection on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

Do I need a state tax release to transfer a parent's Ohio house?

No. The ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms are no longer required. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the probate court clerk what the estate needs.

Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?

Not at that size. For 2026 deaths the federal basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000. Below that, an estate does not need to file Form 706 on account of size.

Can a house pass without full probate in Ohio?

Sometimes. A recorded transfer on death affidavit vests title in the named beneficiary under R.C. 5302.22, and a probate court can release an estate with $35,000 or less in assets under R.C. 2113.03. The probate court can tell you which path fits.

Who owes the county transfer tax on an estate sale in Ohio?

The seller named in the deed. R.C. 322.02 puts the charge on the grantor, payable to the county auditor before the deed reaches the recorder, at a rate each county sets within the thirty-cent cap.

What counts as an Ohio land installment contract

In Ohio it is an executory agreement, not fully performed within a year, in which the seller agrees to convey title and the buyer pays the price in installments while the seller holds title as security. Chapter 5313 of the Revised Code covers it, and R.C. 5313.01 sets the terms. The chapter calls the seller the vendor and the buyer the vendee.

Two limits in the definitions matter. The property must be Ohio real property improved by a dwelling, so a bare lot sale falls outside the chapter. And an option contract to buy real property is expressly not a land installment contract.

The seller can be almost anyone: an individual, partnership, corporation, association, trust, or any other group. An investor who sells on contract is covered by the same chapter as a homeowner who sells to a neighbor.

What the contract must say

The contract is signed in duplicate, and each side keeps a copy. R.C. 5313.02 then lists sixteen items the document must contain at a minimum. The main ones:

  • Full names and current mailing addresses of all parties, and the date each party signed.
  • A legal description of the property, the contract price, any separate service charges, the down payment, and the resulting principal balance.
  • The amount and due date of each installment, plus the interest rate on the unpaid balance and how it is computed.
  • A statement of encumbrances against the property and of any pending order of a public agency.
  • A promise to deliver a general warranty deed on completion, or another available deed if a general warranty deed is not possible.
  • A provision that the seller supply evidence of title under local custom.
  • A provision that, if the seller defaults on a mortgage, the buyer may pay it and get credit on the contract.
  • A provision that the seller will have the contract recorded, and a term making the buyer responsible for taxes and assessments from the contract date unless the parties agree otherwise.

The seller cannot carry a mortgage larger than the balance due on the contract, unless the mortgage covers additional property and the seller disclosed the amount and release price in writing. A seller also cannot place a larger mortgage without the buyer's consent. If the legal description is by metes and bounds, the county engineer reviews it and marks approval on the contract.

Recording the contract

The seller must have a copy recorded under R.C. 5301.25 within twenty days after both parties sign, and must deliver a copy to the county auditor. Recording puts the buyer's interest on the public record at the county recorder, which protects the buyer if the seller later sells or borrows against the same house.

The contract must also follow the formalities Ohio law requires for deeds and mortgages. Each county recorder has its own fee schedule and filing instructions, so call the recorder where the property sits for current requirements.

One duty continues after signing. At least once a year, or on the buyer's demand no more than twice a year, the seller must furnish a statement showing the amount credited to principal and interest and the balance due. A land contract passbook issued by the seller or a financial institution satisfies this. If a seller ignores the chapter, R.C. 5313.04 lets the buyer enforce it in a municipal court, county court or court of common pleas.

When the buyer stops paying

The seller starts by waiting out the cure period. Under R.C. 5313.05, forfeiture can be enforced only after thirty days from the date of default, and a buyer who pays everything currently due, with any charges, inside that window avoids forfeiture.

After the thirty days, the seller serves a written notice. Under R.C. 5313.06 it must identify the contract and the property, list the terms not met, and state that the contract stands forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of completed service. It must also tell the buyer to leave. Service can be by hand, by leaving it at the usual home or at the property, or by registered or certified mail to the last known address.

The route after that depends on how far the buyer has paid:

  • Under five years in, the seller may sue for forfeiture and restitution of the property under Chapter 1923, and serving the 5313.06 notice satisfies the three-day notice rule in R.C. 1923.04(A).
  • At five years of payments, or twenty percent of the price paid, the seller can recover possession only through foreclosure and a judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.
  • In that sale the seller takes proceeds up to the unpaid contract balance.

A judgment for the seller cancels the contract as of a date the court sets. The court clerk sends a certified copy to the county recorder, who records it as an instrument of cancellation. Ending the contract this way is the seller's exclusive remedy, with one exception: if the buyer paid less than fair rental value plus damage to the property, the seller may recover the difference.

Default timeline

Key periods in Ohio Revised Code Chapter 5313
StepPeriod
Record the contract and deliver a copy to the auditor (5313.02(C))Within 20 days after both sign
Statement of balance to buyer (5313.03)At least yearly, no more than twice a year on demand
Cure period after a missed payment (5313.05)30 days from default
Forfeiture notice cure window (5313.06(C))10 days from completed service
Judicial sale required (5313.07)5 years of payments or 20 percent of price paid

A seller who wants to end a contract should check each period against the current statute before sending anything.

Disclosures and sale issues on a land contract house

The residential property disclosure form in R.C. 5302.30 applies to transfers of one-to-four unit residential property made by sale, land installment contract, lease with option to purchase, exchange, or a 99-year renewable lease. A seller on contract completes the form and delivers it to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable. Exempt transfers include those by court order, by a fiduciary administering an estate, between spouses or to lineal relatives, and to a buyer who has lived in the property for a year or more, along with a few others.

If the buyer gets the form or an amendment after signing, the buyer has three business days to rescind in writing, and the right ends by the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. A buyer who never receives the form after making an offer may also rescind within that same outer limit.

Owners who want out of a land contract situation have a few starting points. A seller who holds title and wants to sell the house outright will need the recorded contract, the payment history, and the mortgage payoff. A buyer in default who has paid for several years should talk to a lawyer before leaving, since the five-year and twenty-percent rules can change what the seller may do. Both sides can also cancel their interest together by an instrument recorded under R.C. 5301.331, which Chapter 5313 leaves available.

When a seller on contract wants to cash out, the buyer's rights come first. A cash purchaser will want to see the recorded contract, the payment history and proof of where the buyer stands, and will usually need the buyer's signed release before the deal can close. Gather those papers before you call anyone.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an Ohio land contract buyer have to cure a missed payment?

Thirty days from the date of default. Paying all amounts currently due plus any contract fees within that period stops forfeiture, per R.C. 5313.05.

Can an Ohio seller evict a land contract buyer who has paid for years?

Not by forfeiture alone once the buyer has paid for five years or has paid twenty percent of the price. At that point the seller must use foreclosure and judicial sale under R.C. 2323.07.

Does an Ohio land contract have to be recorded?

Yes. The seller must cause a copy to be recorded and delivered to the county auditor within twenty days after both parties sign, under R.C. 5313.02(C).

What notice does an Ohio seller give before forfeiture?

A written notice that names the contract and property, lists the unmet terms, says the contract is forfeited unless the buyer performs within ten days of service, and tells the buyer to leave. R.C. 5313.06 sets those contents.

Can I rent out or sell a house I am buying on land contract in Ohio?

That depends on the contract terms and the seller's recorded title, which Chapter 5313 leaves to the written agreement. Ask a real estate attorney and the county recorder before listing.

Timeline from filing to move-out

An Ohio eviction typically runs four to six weeks, so a tenant's belongings do not get set out the next day. After the landlord files, the court sends a summons and the hearing usually falls about two weeks later.

Cold weather does not pause the case, and a tenant can be evicted in winter. If you plan to sell, remember that the four to six weeks start only after the written notice has run. The full calendar from notice to an empty house is longer than the court phase alone.

Steps in an Ohio eviction case

Chapter 1923 of the Revised Code, the forcible entry and detainer chapter, sets the order of events. Each step leads to the next, and a landlord who skips one risks dismissal.

  • Written notice to leave, given at least three days before the case begins (R.C. 1923.04).
  • Complaint filed with the municipal or county court that covers the rental address.
  • Summons issued and served, at least seven days before trial (R.C. 1923.06).
  • Hearing before a judge unless a jury is demanded or the case is continued (R.C. 1923.09).
  • Judgment for restitution of the premises plus court costs.
  • Writ of execution requested and carried out by the sheriff, a police officer, a constable or a court bailiff (R.C. 1923.13 and 1923.14).
Ohio eviction stages and timing
StageTiming
Notice to leave (R.C. 1923.04)Three or more days before filing
Service of summons (R.C. 1923.06(A))At least seven days before the trial date
Hearing on possession (R.C. 1923.06(H))No sooner than the seventh day after service is complete
Answer to extra money claims (R.C. 1923.06(H))Twenty-eight days after service is complete
Officer carries out the writ (R.C. 1923.14(A))Within ten days after receiving it

How the summons is served

The clerk always mails the summons and a copy of the complaint by ordinary mail with a certificate of mailing. When filing, the plaintiff chooses a second method: service by a sheriff, a court bailiff or an adult the court designates, or certified mail with return receipt.

The person serving goes to the rental. If the tenant is home, the papers are handed over. If not, they are left with someone of suitable age and discretion at the address. If neither works, a copy is posted in a conspicuous place on the premises. The server must return the process to the clerk within five days and note the method used.

Service is complete once the first two methods are done, or once ordinary mailing and posting have both happened. The summons also warns that a tenant depositing rent with the clerk must keep depositing it until the hearing, that a jury trial may be requested, and that free legal help may be available.

The hearing and the judgment

If no one asks for a jury or a continuance, a judge tries the case, and R.C. 1923.09 allows three outcomes.

  • Complaint true: judgment for restitution of the premises to the landlord, with costs of suit.
  • Complaint true in part: restitution for that part only, with costs divided as the judge sees fit.
  • Complaint not true: judgment against the landlord for costs.

R.C. 1923.081 lets the same trial cover the landlord's claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause. A tenant's request to file an answer, a counterclaim or to take discovery is good cause, and the case then runs like other civil cases. A tenant who needs time to find a lawyer can ask for a continuance, and any agreement reached before the hearing should be in writing and told to the judge.

The writ of eviction after judgment

After a judgment of restitution, the landlord asks the court to issue a writ of execution. A red tag goes up on the door telling the tenant how long remains to leave, generally five days. After that the landlord can ask the officer to set the tenant's things out.

Under R.C. 1923.14, the officer must carry out the writ within ten days after receiving it by restoring the landlord to possession. A tenant who appeals and gets a stay of execution, after posting any required bond, can pause the removal, and the judge then orders the officer to delay further proceedings.

Selling a rented house during an eviction

A pending case does not stop an owner from signing a purchase contract, but the buyer cannot take possession until the tenant leaves voluntarily or the writ is carried out. Buyers who want the house vacant often ask the seller to finish the court process first. Others buy with the tenant in place.

Ohio's self-help ban still applies while the sale is in progress. A landlord may not shut off utilities or lock the tenant out to speed things up (R.C. 5321.15), and a retaliatory possession action can be raised as a defense (R.C. 5321.02).

Manufactured home parks follow their own end steps. If an evicted resident leaves a home unoccupied for three days after judgment, the operator may give the titled owner written notice to remove it within fourteen days. A home worth more than three thousand dollars goes to a sheriff's sale within sixty days of the writ. A home worth three thousand dollars or less can have its title transferred to the plaintiff within thirty days, through the clerk of the common pleas title division.

If the buyer is paying cash and accepts the house as it stands, the closing date can be tied to the date the writ is carried out, so nobody waits on a lender's timetable while the court calendar runs.

Where to get help with an eviction case

Start with the clerk of the court named on the summons. The clerk can explain local filing and hearing procedures but cannot give legal advice. Free legal aid is listed by county, and Akron, Cleveland, Columbus and Toledo have Right to Counsel programs for some tenants with low income. Owners with several rentals often hire a landlord attorney, because a missed deadline can force a restart of the notice and filing sequence. Keep a file with the lease, the rent ledger, the notice, proof of delivery and every court paper, since the judge and the buyer will both ask for them.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a tenant have to leave after an Ohio eviction judgment?

The posted red tag generally allows five days. After that the landlord can ask the sheriff or bailiff to carry out the writ, which the officer must execute within ten days after receiving it.

Can a landlord evict a tenant in the winter in Ohio?

Yes. Evictions can happen in winter or very cold weather. The case follows the same notice, hearing and writ steps as in any other season.

What is the earliest an Ohio eviction hearing can be held?

No sooner than the seventh day after service of the summons is complete, under R.C. 1923.06(H). Service must be made at least seven days before the day set for trial.

Can a landlord collect back rent in the same Ohio case?

Often yes. R.C. 1923.081 allows the trial to include claims for past due rent and other damages, unless the court continues those claims for good cause such as a tenant's request to answer or take discovery.

Does an eviction filing stop a sale of the house?

No. An owner can still sell, but possession depends on the tenant leaving or the writ being carried out. A buyer who wants a vacant house usually asks the seller to complete the court process before closing.

What an Ohio quitclaim deed transfers

A quitclaim hands over whatever the signer holds and nothing beyond it. R.C. 5301.02 treats a grant of land as conveying the full interest the grantor can lawfully pass, unless the deed plainly shows a smaller estate was meant. Quitclaim wording adds no extra title. A grantor who owns half gives the grantee half.

The Revised Code prints statutory forms for three other deed types, each with named promises. The general warranty form in R.C. 5302.05 carries covenants that the grantor owns the land in fee simple, that nothing encumbers it, and that the grantor will defend the title against all claims. The limited warranty form in 5302.07 shrinks those promises to claims arising through the grantor. The fiduciary form in 5302.09 serves executors, administrators, trustees, guardians and receivers.

Covenants only come along when the deed says so. Under R.C. 5302.06 the phrase "general warranty covenants" brings in the full list of promises. Leave that phrase out and the buyer is relying on the title the grantor actually has.

Signing, witnessing and what the deed should contain

The grantor's signature has to be acknowledged. R.C. 5301.01 lists who can take the acknowledgment: a judge or clerk of a state court of record, the county auditor, the county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. That official certifies it over his or her own signature. Most owners just visit a notary.

The statutory forms show what a tidy Ohio deed looks like. It names the grantor with marital status and county, recites consideration, gives the grantee's tax-mailing address, describes the land, cites the earlier recorded instrument by volume and page, and includes dower release language for a spouse. Those elements make a sound checklist for any deed you prepare.

One duty catches sellers of troubled houses. Under R.C. 5301.253, an owner who has received a written building or housing code violation notice must give the grantee written notice of those violations before any transfer agreement is made. With no written agreement, the notice is due before the deed is filed. A notice already sitting in an issuing authority's public records also follows the property to later owners without a fresh order.

Where an Ohio deed is filed and what the recorder charges

Take the deed to the recorder in the county where the parcel lies, as R.C. 5301.25 directs. Skipping this leaves a gap: an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who paid in good faith and knew nothing of it.

The recorder's price list is in R.C. 317.32. For recording and indexing a standard instrument, the statute prints these charges:

  • Seventeen dollars as a base fee plus seventeen dollars as a housing trust fund fee covers the first two pages.
  • Every later page adds four dollars of each.
  • A county may add a preservation surcharge of no more than five dollars.

The auditor looks at the deed before the recorder does. If a surveyor drew the land, the auditor requires the deed to name the surveyor in one short sentence: "A survey of this property was made by" followed by the name.

Who pays the conveyance fee on a quitclaim?

The person giving up title pays. Under R.C. 319.202, the grantor covers the state-set fee plus any county transfer tax when the statement of value reaches the auditor. R.C. 319.54 sets the mandatory fee at one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is higher.

A county can pile its own tax on top. R.C. 322.02 allows up to thirty cents per hundred dollars, charged to the grantor and paid to the auditor before the deed goes to the recorder. Ask your auditor whether your county levies it.

The definition of "value" matters. On a sale it means everything paid, including any mortgage balance. On a gift in whole or part it means the price the land would likely bring on the open market. Deliberately misstating value is forbidden. Separately, a fifty-cent charge applies to each transfer or entry on the auditor's books and is paid by whoever requests it.

Transfers exempt from the conveyance fee

Quite a few are, and several match what families do with quitclaims. When an exemption fits, the form only needs a short note giving the reason.

Selected exemptions under R.C. 319.54(G)(3)
Type of transferLetter in the statute
Confirming or correcting a deed already recorded(c)
Gift between spouses, or from parent to child or the spouse of either(d)
Made under court order, when not a result of a sale under that order(f)
No money or other valuable consideration paid, and not a gift(m)
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent with no money paid(s)
To a trustee when the grantor kept an unlimited power to revoke(t)
Sale for delinquent taxes or assessments(e)

The full list in section 319.54 is longer. It also reaches government transfers, transfers that only secure or release a debt, and assorted corporate and trust moves.

Survivorship and transfer on death instead of a quitclaim

When a family wants a transfer to take effect at death, Ohio offers statutory tools that a plain quitclaim cannot match. R.C. 5302.20 creates a survivorship tenancy when a deed or will shows clear intent that the survivor takes everything. The word "or" between two grantees is not enough alone. If fewer than all survivorship tenants convey to an outsider, the grantor's interest passes only if the grantor survives.

A transfer on death designation affidavit under R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner name beneficiaries who take title at death. No payment and no handoff to the beneficiary is needed. The affidavit must be on file with the recorder before the owner dies, at the same recording price as a deed, and it is sworn before someone authorized to administer oaths.

Two more survivorship rules touch family deeds. A conveyance from every survivorship tenant to another person, or from all but one of them to the remaining tenant, ends the tenancy and vests title in the grantee. And if the only two tenants are spouses whose marriage ends by divorce, annulment or dissolution, the title becomes a tenancy in common unless the judgment says survivorship continues.

A quitclaim made now gives the grantee a present interest, and the exemptions in the table above cover family gifts. By any route, a deed does not clear taxes. The lien statute keeps the year's claim on the parcel until it is paid. If you plan to sell, get the treasurer's payoff figure before you sign anything.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Ohio house with a quitclaim deed?

Yes, any signed, acknowledged and recorded deed can carry a sale. The buyer gets only the title you hold, with none of the covenants a warranty form carries. Ask your title company which form the buyer's lender will accept.

Does an Ohio quitclaim deed have to be notarized?

The signature must be acknowledged before an official the statute names, and a notary public is one of them. Most owners use a notary.

Will a quitclaim deed erase a mortgage or tax lien in Ohio?

No. The year's tax lien attaches on January 1 and stays until paid, no matter who holds title. Get payoff numbers from the treasurer and your lender before you transfer.

Is there a conveyance fee on a deed between relatives?

Gifts between spouses, and gifts from a parent to a child or a child's spouse, are on the exempt list. So is a transfer where nothing of value changes hands and it is not a gift. The form carries a short statement of the reason.

Where do I record an Ohio quitclaim deed?

Bring it to the recorder in the county that holds the parcel, once the auditor has endorsed it. Until then a later good faith buyer can win out over it. The recorder's office can quote its charges.

What an Ohio transfer on death designation affidavit is

It is a sworn document naming who gets an Ohio home or other real estate when the owner dies, with no probate transfer of that parcel. The authority is Revised Code 5302.22, with companion rules in sections 5302.222 and 5302.23.

The affidavit works only if it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death. No buyer's signature is needed, no payment, and no delivery to the person named. Ohio law also treats a transfer made this way as not testamentary, so for that property it outranks a will or the intestacy rules.

Some owners confuse this with a transfer on death deed. Ohio's current statute calls the instrument an affidavit. The older deed form survives only for designations made before the 2009 change.

Who can sign and what goes in the affidavit

Sole owners, tenants in common and survivorship tenants may sign, and a married owner signs jointly with the spouse. The designation can cover the whole interest or a stated fraction.

Someone authorized to administer oaths must verify the signing. Division (D) of section 5302.22 calls for these items:

  • A legal description of the land, with a pointer to a recorded instrument that contains it.
  • A statement of the exact part being passed, if it is less than everything.
  • The signer's statement that the record shows the signer as owner at the time of recording, along with marital status.
  • For a married signer, the spouse's statement that dower rights give way to the beneficiary's title.
  • One or more beneficiaries, each named individually.

A knowingly false statement is falsification under division (A)(6) of section 2921.13. Recorders do not draft documents, so most owners hire an attorney or use a title company.

Recording the affidavit and the cost

The owner brings it to the recorder in the county where the land sits. The recorder files it the way a deed is filed, charges the deed fee, and indexes it under the signing owner's name.

Section 317.32 splits each charge into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. A county may also add a document preservation surcharge capped at $5, so the final bill varies by county. Ask the recorder for the all-in number before you send a check.

Recording charge for a deed-type document, R.C. 317.32(A)(1)
Charge componentFirst two pagesEach later page
Base fee$17$4
Housing trust fund fee$17$4
Preservation surchargeUp to $5 per document, set by the county

Local practice can add a step. In Pickaway County, a transfer on death designation cannot be mailed in, because it needs auditor and engineer stamps first and must be carried to the office.

Ownership while the owner is alive

Nothing changes. Section 5302.23 gives the designation no effect on present ownership, and the named beneficiary holds no interest until the owner dies. The owner can still sell, mortgage, lease or live in the house.

For a seller this means a buyer's title company will see the recorded affidavit in the chain of title, but you can convey by deed without the beneficiary's consent. When a deed to a buyer is recorded, the affidavit has nothing left to act on.

Lienholders are unaffected as well. A mortgagee, judgment creditor or mechanic's lien holder keeps every right it had, and it need not name the beneficiary in a foreclosure unless that person holds some other interest in the land.

Changing or revoking the designation

An owner can do it at any time without the beneficiary's consent. Record a new transfer on death designation affidavit stating the change, and the later-recorded one supersedes every earlier recorded affidavit for that property.

The statute also builds in several automatic effects:

  • If a named beneficiary dies first and a contingent beneficiary was named, the contingent person takes the same share.
  • If no named beneficiary survives and none is contingent, the interest falls into the owner's probate estate.
  • Several beneficiaries take equal shares as tenants in common unless the affidavit says otherwise or makes them survivorship tenants.
  • If the owner's spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, the spouse is treated as having died before the owner.

A recorded affidavit also keeps dower rights from vesting in a spouse the owner marries afterward, unless the designation is changed or revoked.

What the beneficiary files after the owner dies

The beneficiary signs an affidavit of confirmation. Under Section 5302.222, the beneficiary presents it to the auditor of the county where the land lies and then files it with that county's recorder. A notary or other oath-giver verifies it, and a certified copy of the death certificate goes with it.

The statute fixes its contents: each surviving beneficiary's name and address, the date the owner died, the property description, and the names of any beneficiaries who did not survive. For each one who died first, a certified death certificate is attached too.

Land under the Chapter 5309 registration system follows a separate route in section 5309.081. In every case the beneficiary receives only what the owner held at death, along with each mortgage, reservation or exception already tied to the land.

Conveyance fee on a transfer on death

Often there is none, though the auditor makes the call. The list in section 319.54(G)(3) exempts, among others, a transfer where no money or other valuable and tangible consideration changes hands and that is not a gift. For an exempt transfer, section 319.202 asks only for a statement of the reason.

The form family is DTE 100. In Paulding County the auditor uses DTE 100 (EX) to claim an exemption, while Pickaway County will not transfer anything without a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX. Check with your own auditor before filing an affidavit of confirmation.

Recording is billed separately from anything the auditor takes, at the same rate as a deed.

Selling a house with a recorded affidavit

It can be sold. While the owner lives, the owner signs a deed and closing goes ahead as usual. After the owner has died, the beneficiary must record the affidavit of confirmation before a deed to any buyer will clear the auditor and the recorder.

Skipping an estate for this parcel can save weeks. The beneficiary still carries the mortgage balance, any back property tax, needed repairs and co-owners, because the property arrives burdened by whatever is on record.

An heir who wants to sell an Ohio house as-is for cash should expect the buyer to ask for the recorded affidavit of confirmation first.

Frequently asked questions

Does a transfer on death affidavit keep a house out of probate in Ohio?

For the covered parcel, yes. Section 5302.23 makes the transfer non-testamentary and overrides a will or an intestate transfer of that property. A parcel with no surviving named or contingent beneficiary lands in the probate estate.

Does the beneficiary have to sign?

No. Under 5302.22(F) the affidavit needs no payment and no delivery to the beneficiary. It takes effect once recorded with the county recorder during the owner's life.

May an owner name a trust as the beneficiary?

Yes. A beneficiary may be a natural or legal person, such as a bank serving as trustee. If a successor trustee replaces the named trustee before the owner dies, the successor stands in, and the affidavit of confirmation lists that successor.

What happens if the owner was married when signing?

The spouse signs too, and the spouse's dower rights give way to the beneficiary's title. If the spouse is the beneficiary and the marriage later ends by divorce, dissolution or annulment, that designation ends.

Can a lender still foreclose on a house with a recorded affidavit?

Yes. Lienholders keep every right, and the beneficiary inherits subject to existing encumbrances. A lender suing to foreclose need not name the beneficiary unless that person has some other interest in the land.

Seller closing costs in Ohio

An Ohio seller's bill at closing has two parts: a few charges written into the Revised Code, and whatever the purchase contract hands to the seller. The statutory items are the county auditor's conveyance fee, an optional county transfer tax, a small per-parcel transfer fee and, on paper filings, any recording charge the contract puts on you. The contract side covers your mortgage payoff and prorations for taxes and similar items.

Use the table as a checklist of the charges the legislature set, then ask the title agent for the line items on your own closing statement.

Ohio charges set by statute that touch a home sale
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee, paid to the county auditor (R.C. 319.54(G)(3))$1 or ten cents per $100 or fraction, whichever is greater
Optional county real property transfer tax (R.C. 322.02(A))Up to thirty cents per $100
Auditor's entry of a land transfer (R.C. 319.54(G)(2))Fifty cents per transfer
Recording the first two pages of an instrument (R.C. 317.32(A))$17 base plus $17 housing trust fund
Each added page (R.C. 317.32(A))$4 base plus $4 housing trust fund
Optional document preservation surcharge (R.C. 317.32(A))Up to $5 per instrument

Who pays the conveyance fee

The grantor, which means the seller. Section 319.202 puts the fee under 319.54(G)(3), plus any Chapter 322 transfer tax, on the grantor at the moment the deed is delivered. The deed makes two stops, the auditor first and the recorder second.

The fee is figured on "value." That means everything paid or promised for the property, with any mortgage or vendor's lien counted in. For a gift, value is the open-market price a willing buyer and willing seller would agree on. Willfully falsifying the stated value is prohibited.

Do Ohio counties charge different conveyance rates?

Yes. The state sets the floor. Commissioners in each county may add up to thirty cents per hundred dollars under section 322.02. To adopt it, the board must hold two public hearings and publish notice, and the resolution is generally open to a referendum.

Two counties show how the printed figure looks. Morrow County shows $4.00 per thousand for real estate and for manufactured homes alike. Muskingum County prints the same $4.00 per thousand. Its method is the sale price times 0.004, rounded to the nearest ten cents, with a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee added. Rates vary elsewhere, so check your own county auditor's real estate transfer page or phone the office before you estimate proceeds.

Transfers that skip the conveyance fee

The exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3) matter most to families and estates. They include:

  • A deed whose only purpose is to confirm or correct one already recorded.
  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a parent to a child or the child's spouse.
  • A transfer among heirs at law or devisees of a common decedent when no money is paid.
  • A deed to the trustee of a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke.
  • A transfer that involves no money or other valuable consideration and is not a gift.
  • A transfer by court order, unless it results from a sale made under that order.
  • An interest worth $100 or less.

For an exempt transfer, the statement of value only has to give the reason for the exemption.

Recording fees

The recorder's charges come from section 317.32, and the base and housing trust fund amounts are the same in every county. Pages are counted by the caption page and any partial page, measured at eight and one-half by fourteen inches, so a deed with exhibits costs more than a short one.

Fees are due when the instrument is presented, except electronic filings, which may be settled afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method. The statute leaves open which side of a sale pays for recording the deed. Read your purchase contract, or ask the title agent, to see who is assigned that line.

Property tax proration at closing

Ohio real estate taxes come in two installments, and the default due dates in section 323.12 are December 31 and June 20. Counties set their own closing dates, which can differ.

On a sale, the owner of record receives the bill, and taxes should be prorated at closing. The seller credits the buyer for the prorated share on the closing statement. Muskingum County's treasurer describes it that way, and other counties work much the same. Your title agent computes the actual figure.

Two other items can surface in the deed's statement of value. If the home received a tax reduction under section 323.152, the statement must address it. If the land was in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program, a recoupment charge under section 5713.34 may apply when it stops qualifying.

Mortgage payoff and the lien release

Your payoff is taken from the sale proceeds and sent to the lender. Under section 5301.36, the lender must then record a release of the mortgage within ninety days of satisfaction, and the contract can let it recover the recording fee from the borrower.

If no release is recorded, the owner can send a written notice. The lender then has fifteen days before damages of $100 per day begin, capped at $5,000. A mortgagor may also recover $250 in damages for a late release. After closing, look up the county recorder's index to confirm the release posted.

Seller disclosures

Sellers of homes with as many as four dwelling units fill out the state's property disclosure form and give the buyer a signed copy, as section 5302.30 requires. The form covers water supply, sewer, structure, hazardous materials and known defects.

If the form reaches the buyer only after the contract is signed, the buyer has three business days to back out. That right ends at the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or closing. Exceptions cover court-ordered transfers, estate fiduciary transfers, and a seller who inherited the home and has not lived there in the past year. When the buyer is borrowing, federal rules require the lender to provide a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing, and its seller-side lines show credits and prorations.

What a seller gets back at closing

A closing statement runs both directions. Besides charges, a seller can be owed money, most often a refund of taxes or other items prepaid beyond the closing date. The buyer's Closing Disclosure shows costs the seller prepaid that the buyer reimburses, and prior taxes and fees the seller owes that the buyer will pay later and the seller covers now. Tax prorations land on those lines.

A seller may also agree to contribute to the buyer's closing costs, either as a general amount or as named "Seller Paid" items. If you offer a credit to win a sale, have the figure written into the contract and carried to the final statement so the two match.

Your net is the sale price less the payoff, the statutory fees above, any agreed credits and the tax proration. Ask the title agent for a draft statement several days before closing, then compare each line against the table on this page and the county's printed rate. A cash sale tends to trim the list, since there is no lender-driven paperwork on the buyer's side to wait on.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Ohio conveyance fee?

Revised Code 319.54(G)(3) sets it at the greater of $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value. A county can layer up to thirty cents per hundred on top, and both land on the seller.

Does Ohio have a state transfer tax?

Ohio's charge is collected by the county auditor rather than as one flat state rate. The statutory fee has a floor, and counties may levy an optional tax capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars.

Who pays recording fees on an Ohio sale?

The statute sets the amount and leaves the assignment to the contract. Check the settlement statement or ask the title agent which side carries the deed's recording fee.

How fast must an Ohio lender record the mortgage release?

Within ninety days after the mortgage is satisfied. If it is late, the owner can give written notice, and the lender then has fifteen days to record before daily damages start.

Are inherited-house sales exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?

Sometimes. The disclosure statute exempts a seller who got the property by inheritance and has not lived in it within the past year, as well as transfers by estate fiduciaries.

How unpaid Ohio property tax becomes a lien

The lien exists from the first day of each tax year. R.C. 323.11 says the state's lien for real property tax attaches on January 1 and lasts until the tax, penalties, interest and charges are paid. Your bill arrives later, but the claim on the parcel is already there.

That is why an unpaid balance cannot simply be left behind at a closing. If only part of a tract changes hands, the same section lets the tax be apportioned, and the lien then reaches each part only up to the amount allocated to it.

The county treasurer, working through the prosecuting attorney, files the foreclosure case. The owner gets several chances to pay before the property is sold.

When an Ohio county starts tax foreclosure

The treasurer may sue once taxes have gone unpaid for sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered to the treasurer. R.C. 323.25 lets the treasurer enforce the lien by civil action, the way a mortgage is foreclosed, in common pleas court, in a municipal court with jurisdiction, or before the county Board of Revision where that board has authority.

A second route appears in R.C. 5721.18. The prosecuting attorney files in the treasurer's name after the auditor delivers the delinquent land certificate or master list. An in rem action, one against the parcel itself, may be filed once the second year has ended from the date the delinquency was first certified.

The treasurer is barred from enforcing the lien in any of these situations:

  • The parcel has a pending application for exemption and is not on the delinquent land duplicate.
  • A valid delinquent tax contract is in force and has not been voided.
  • A tax certificate on the parcel has been sold, as to the taxes it covers.

Stopping a tax foreclosure

Pay the delinquency or arrange a plan. R.C. 323.31 entitles an owner who lives in the home, or a land contract buyer who occupies it, to at least one written delinquent tax contract with the treasurer, provided no tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment is outstanding. Residential contracts run up to five years, and at least two years if the owner asks. Any later contract is up to the treasurer.

You may sign the contract any time before the adjudication of foreclosure. It breaks if an installment is missed or the current taxes go unpaid, and the prosecuting attorney then files the foreclosure. If a tax certificate was sold, the owner uses a redemption payment plan under section 5721.38 instead.

The right to redeem stays open for a while after suit is filed. R.C. 5721.25 lets anyone entitled to redeem pay the taxes, assessments, penalties, interest, charges and costs to the treasurer before foreclosure begins. After filing, redemption remains possible until the entry confirming the sale, or until the alternative redemption period ends, but the owner must also show the property meets zoning, land use, building, health and safety codes. A delinquent tax contract can even be signed after filing, for up to five years, though the case keeps moving and the contract can end if the property falls out of code compliance.

Alternative redemption period and abandoned land

This is a short window after judgment. R.C. 323.65 defines it as twenty-eight days after the adjudication of foreclosure is journalized, ending on and including the twenty-eighth day. When it runs out, the owner's right and equity of redemption end with no further order. A county treasurer decides whether to invoke it under section 323.78.

If it is invoked and a city, township, county, school district, community development organization or land reutilization corporation has asked for the parcel, the court or board orders it deeded to that body without appraisal or sale, free of the taxes and other liens. If nobody asked, the parcel is sold in the usual way, and if no one bids it is forfeited to the state.

The expedited process for abandoned land turns on the word unoccupied. A parcel counts as unoccupied when no taxable building is lived in, no trade or business operates there, or the parcel is uninhabited with no sign of changed tenants or improvements. A presumption arises when the parcel is not agricultural and at least two of these are true at certification:

  • An exterior inspection by the county, municipality or township finds no person, trade or business present.
  • No utility connections serve it, or none are being billed.
  • It is boarded up or sealed after being found open, vacant or vandalized.
  • It is insecure, vacant or vandalized on visible inspection.

Stages of a county tax foreclosure

Ohio delinquent land tax enforcement, stage by stage
StageTiming or limit
Lien attachesJanuary 1 of each tax year
Suit by the treasurerAfter 60 days from delivery of the delinquent duplicate
Answer in an in rem actionWithin 28 days after service is complete
Payment planUp to 5 years for an owner-occupied home
Alternative redemption28 days after judgment is journalized
Second sale if no bidNot less than 2 or more than 6 weeks later

In an in rem case the answer deadline is the one to watch. Section 5721.18 allows a default judgment on any parcel without an answer, and it binds everyone with an interest, including people out of state.

Under R.C. 5721.19, the court may order a parcel sold without appraisal for no less than the lesser of two figures: the auditor's fair market value plus costs, or the total found due plus costs. If no bid reaches that figure, the sale is adjourned to a second date. If a sale brings in less than what is owed, the court may enter a deficiency judgment against the owner of record. A sale in an in rem case under division (B) gives the buyer title free of most liens, apart from a properly filed federal tax lien and earlier easements and covenants.

Selling the house or collecting leftover money

A sale does not end a case already filed. R.C. 5721.18(D) provides that a conveyance after the complaint is filed and before the foreclosure judgment does not cancel the county's right to proceed. Ask the treasurer and the prosecuting attorney for a payoff figure that includes the costs of the case, have it paid from the proceeds at closing, and get written confirmation that the case is resolved.

A sale of land for delinquent taxes carries no auditor's conveyance fee under R.C. 319.54, which lists transfers on sale for delinquent taxes among its exemptions.

When a foreclosure sale brings in more than the judgment, R.C. 5721.20 sends the excess to the clerk of court within forty-five days after confirmation, and the clerk notifies the owner. Money unclaimed within ninety days of the final notice goes to the county treasury, where the treasurer holds it for three years. After that it is forfeited to the delinquent tax and assessment collection fund, or to a land reutilization fund where the county has one.

Frequently asked questions

How long can I be behind on Ohio property tax before foreclosure?

The treasurer may sue sixty days after the delinquent land duplicate is delivered. A prosecuting attorney in rem action can follow after the second year from first certification. The treasurer can tell you where your parcel stands.

Can I set up a payment plan for delinquent Ohio taxes?

Yes. An owner who lives in the home is entitled to at least one delinquent tax contract, running up to five years, or two if requested. No tax lien certificate or foreclosure judgment can be outstanding when the first contract is signed.

Can I still pay after the county files a tax foreclosure?

Yes. You can redeem by paying everything due plus costs before the entry confirming the sale, or before the alternative redemption period of twenty-eight days after judgment ends. The property must also meet local building and zoning codes.

What does the alternative redemption period mean?

It is the twenty-eight days after the court or Board of Revision journalizes the foreclosure judgment. Once it ends, the owner's right of redemption is gone with no further order. Only counties whose treasurer invokes it use it.

Do I get money back if my house sells for more than the taxes owed?

Yes. Excess proceeds go to the clerk, who notifies the owner. If it goes unclaimed for ninety days after the final notice, the county treasurer holds it, and the owner may demand it within three years.
